title: Checking an installation plan by hand

blocks.text: A museum plans the installation of its new exhibitions. Each job needs some installers for some days; some jobs, the noisy or dusty ones, must happen while their gallery is closed to visitors. The museum has a fixed team of installers. Days are numbered from 0, and a job that starts on day `s` and takes `d` days occupies days `s` to `s + d - 1` and ends at `s + d`.

Write `broken_rules(jobs, start, installers, horizon)` in `checker.py`, **without a solver**: it checks a plan someone else made. `jobs` maps a job to `(days, installers_needed, windows)`, where `windows` is a list of closures `(a, b)`, each the half-open span of days $`[a, b)`$ (open from the start of day `a` to the start of day `b`), or `None` when the job can happen any time. `start` maps each job to its start day. Return the set of broken rules:

items: `("outside", job)` when the job starts before day 0 or ends after `horizon`;
`("window", job)` when the job has windows and lies wholly inside none of them;
`("crowded", day)` for each day `t` from 0 to `horizon - 1` on which the installers needed by the jobs running exceed `installers`.

blocks.text: The rules, with $`s_j`$, $`d_j`$, $`n_j`$ and $`\mathcal{W}_j`$ each job's start, days, installers and windows, $`N`$ the team and $`H`$ the horizon:
Write each rule the plain way, one loop per rule. The tests hand you plans that break known rules. About fifteen lines.

cases.says: a plan that keeps every rule gets an empty set
a job that starts before day 0 or ends after the horizon is reported as outside
a job that ends exactly when its window ends is inside the window, and one that runs a day longer is not
a day is crowded when the installers the running jobs need exceed the team, even if few jobs run

origin.section: A Checker Written From the Rules Proves the Schedule

concepts: a checker written from the rules in plain Python verifies any schedule and must be shown to fail
